title: Rabbi Abba bar Zevina
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: His father was a sage in the city of Tyre and was appointed on condition that he return [to the Land of Israel], as in Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim 3:3. His son Rabbi Abba was the distinguished student of Rabbi Zeira (I): he attended Rabbi Zeira, as in Berakhot 7:3; went with him to the bathhouse, as in Shabbat 7:9; spoke in Rabbi Zeira’s name, as in Rosh Hashanah 3:3, 3:6 and 4:6 and Shekalim 4:1; and with his colleague Rabbi Yonah in Rabbi Zeira’s name, as in Berakhot 7:5, Demai 3:1 and Bereshit Rabbah 60:8. At the end of Berakhot, chapter 6, he relates of Rabbi Zeira that he would mention [a phrase] corresponding to the occasion. His well-known saying is in Demai 3:3: “Rabbi Abba bar Zevina said in Rabbi Zeira’s name: If the early ones were sons of angels, we are human beings,” etc. This saying is repeated in Shekalim 5:1, where it reads bar Zemina; in Bereshit Rabbah 60:8 in the name of bar Yemina, and Hyman proposes Zemina; and in Shabbat 112b the saying reads “Rabbi Zeira said that Rava bar Zemina said,” and Hyman proposes the reverse.
Likewise we find that he spoke in the name of (attributed it to) Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa, as in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 4:1, Megillah 3:5 and Taanit 4:1;
in the name of Rabbi Oshaya, Jerusalem Talmud Kiddushin 4:1 and Sanhedrin 6:7; in the name of Rabbi Elazar, who said that Rabbi Oshayah said, Taanit 1:3;

in the name of (attributed to) Rabbi Dosa the Elder, Jerusalem Talmud Chagigah 1:8 and the end of Sanhedrin, chapter 10. He likewise cites the dispute between Rabbi Chelbo and Rabbi Chama bar Chanina, Kilayim 9:4; and in the name of Rabbi Yehotzadak, Sheviit, beginning of chapter 9, and Beitzah, beginning of chapter 1;

in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak, Jerusalem Talmud Sheviit, beginning of chapter 9. His livelihood was from the work of tailoring, and he sewed shoes, as in Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 9:5, where Rabbi Zeira his teacher instructed him to tell Bar Rishon (the tailor’s name; the Shenot Eliyahu there reads Bar Rishon) not to sew him a shoe with linen [thread]; the Ahavat Tziyon ViYerushalayim there cites another reading. In Jerusalem Talmud Sheviit 4:2: once he was working as a tailor with an Aramean in the town of Rome (a town Rome in the Land of Israel), and he brought him carcass meat and said to him, “Eat, or else I will kill you.” He said to him, “If you wish, kill me, and I will not eat.” Then the gentile said to him: “Who told you that had you eaten the carcass I would have killed you? Either a Jew [should be] a Jew, or an Aramean an Aramean” (each nation must keep its religion). Rabbi Mana said of this: had Rabbi Abba bar Zevina heard the law that for all transgressions in private one should transgress and not be killed, except for three, he would have eaten the carcass.
He is likewise mentioned in Jerusalem Talmud Bava Metzia 5:6: he would give a dinar to a shopkeeper and take from him [produce] all year at the cheap season’s price.

notes.text: על מנת לחזור means appointment conditional on RETURNING to the Land, not returning a payment, supported by Guggenheimer Bikkurim3:3. בביתן is read בכיתן, LINEN thread, supported by its Kilayim9:4; retain Hyman’s9:5 alongside it. השם is read בשם and the duplicated Shabbat clause is translated once, as previously disclosed. Zevina/Zemina/Yemina and teacher-chain reversals remain Hyman’s variants/proposals. His Palestinian Rome parenthetical and meat refusal narrative are retained.

The consulted Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim 3:3 concerns appointment abroad on condition of returning, and names Zemina in Tyre. Kilayim 9:4 has Zeira instruct Abba bar Zemina to tell Bar Rishon not to sew his shoe with linen but with a strap; Hyman supplies 9:5. These support the disclosed return and linen readings, without independently admitting the father/son identification, Zevina/Zemina/Yemina equivalences, or Hyman’s reversal of the Shabbat reporting chain. The Palestinian Rome parenthetical and meat-refusal account remain his account; exact Shenot Eliyahu and Ahavat Tziyon ViYerushalayim readings have not been inspected here.
